metadata.notes: Autonomous STRIDE analysis based on architecture documentation. No interactive interview conducted.

participants.coverageNotes: Single-perspective analysis from security architecture viewpoint. No developer, operations, business stakeholder, or GIS domain expert input. Coverage gaps exist in: operational risk assessment, business impact calibration, GIS-specific attack technique knowledge, and deployment-specific threat identification.

actors.name: External Attacker
actors.motivation: Data theft, service disruption, resource abuse, or lateral movement

actors.name: Malicious Insider
actors.motivation: Data exfiltration, sabotage, or unauthorized access escalation

threats.title: No authentication architecture — all endpoints accessible to anonymous users
threats.description: No authentication mechanism is specified anywhere in the architecture. The GraphQL API accepts queries and mutations — including dataset upload and deletion — from any network client without identity verification. An attacker can upload malicious datasets, query all stored data, and delete datasets without attribution.
recommendedMitigations: Implement OAuth2/OIDC with a proven identity provider (Auth0, Keycloak, or cloud-native)
Require authentication on all GraphQL mutations
Require authentication on sensitive queries (dataset listing, feature queries)
Consider allowing anonymous read-only access to public datasets only
threats.residualRisk: Low — standard auth implementation addresses this fully

threats.title: No service-to-service authentication between internal components
threats.description: No mTLS, shared secrets, or service mesh authentication is specified between API, Martin, PgBouncer, Redis, or Celery. If an attacker gains access to the internal network (via container escape, SSRF, or compromised dependency), they can impersonate any service.
existingControls: Docker Compose network isolation (dev only)
recommendedMitigations: Use password authentication for PostgreSQL connections through PgBouncer
Enable Redis AUTH
Consider mTLS or service mesh for production deployment
Use separate database credentials per service with least-privilege grants

threats.title: GraphQL introspection exposes full API schema to unauthenticated clients
threats.description: GraphQL introspection is enabled by default in Strawberry. Without explicit disabling, any client can query __schema to discover all types, queries, mutations, and fields — providing a detailed reconnaissance map for attackers.
recommendedMitigations: Disable GraphQL introspection in production
If introspection is needed for tooling, restrict to authenticated admin users
Implement persisted queries to limit query shapes

threats.title: No API key or token management for programmatic access
threats.description: No mechanism exists for API consumers to authenticate programmatically. Without API keys, tokens, or client certificates, there is no way to identify, rate-limit, or revoke programmatic clients independently from browser users.
recommendedMitigations: Implement API key issuance and validation for programmatic clients
Support bearer token authentication (JWT or opaque tokens)
Implement per-key rate limiting and usage tracking
Provide key revocation capability

threats.title: Malicious GeoJSON properties enable stored XSS in frontend
threats.description: GeoJSON feature properties are arbitrary JSON objects stored verbatim in PostGIS and rendered in the frontend feature inspector. An attacker uploads a GeoJSON file where property values contain HTML or JavaScript payloads. When another user inspects these features on the map, the payload executes in their browser.
existingControls: React JSX auto-escaping (partial — does not cover dangerouslySetInnerHTML or href attributes)
recommendedMitigations: Sanitize all feature property values at ingestion time — strip HTML tags and script content
Never use dangerouslySetInnerHTML to render feature properties
Implement Content Security Policy (CSP) to mitigate XSS impact
Encode property values when rendering in DOM attributes (href, src, style)

threats.title: Shapefile ZIP archive path traversal writes files outside extraction directory
threats.description: Shapefiles are distributed as ZIP archives. A crafted ZIP with entries like '../../etc/cron.d/backdoor' or '../../app/config.py' could write files anywhere on the filesystem accessible to the extraction process, potentially overwriting application code or configuration.
existingControls: CODING-CONVENTIONS.md: 'Prevent path traversal during archive extraction'
INITIAL-PLAN.md: 'Handle archive extraction carefully for Shapefile uploads'
recommendedMitigations: Validate all ZIP entry paths before extraction — reject entries containing '..' or absolute paths
Use Python's zipfile module with explicit path joining and canonicalization
Extract to an isolated temporary directory with restricted permissions
Validate extracted files match expected Shapefile structure before processing

threats.title: No integrity verification on files between storage and processing
threats.description: After upload, raw files are stored in object storage and later read by Celery workers for ingestion. If object storage is compromised or a race condition exists, the file processed may differ from what was uploaded. No checksums or integrity verification is documented.
recommendedMitigations: Compute and store SHA-256 hash at upload time
Verify hash before processing in Celery worker
Store hash in dataset record in PostGIS

threats.title: Redis without AUTH allows cache poisoning and job manipulation
threats.description: Redis serves as both query cache and Celery broker. Without authentication, any process on the network can: (1) poison cached query results to serve incorrect spatial data, (2) inject malicious Celery tasks, (3) modify pending task arguments, (4) flush the entire cache causing a thundering herd on PostGIS.
recommendedMitigations: Enable Redis AUTH with a strong password
Use Redis ACLs to separate cache and broker access patterns
Bind Redis to localhost or internal network only
Monitor Redis for unexpected command patterns

threats.title: No TLS between internal services — data modifiable in transit
threats.description: Inter-service communication (API to PostgreSQL, Martin to PostgreSQL, API to Redis, Celery to Redis) uses unencrypted protocols. An attacker with network access can modify SQL queries, spatial data, or cache contents in transit.
recommendedMitigations: Enable TLS for all PostgreSQL connections
Enable TLS for Redis connections
Use encrypted overlay networks in production (Docker Swarm encrypted overlay, Kubernetes network policies with encryption)

threats.title: Crafted GeoParquet payloads exploit DuckDB Arrow/Parquet parser
threats.description: DuckDB processes GeoParquet files using native Arrow/Parquet parsers within the Celery worker process. Crafted Parquet files with malformed column metadata, invalid compression blocks, or oversized allocations could trigger buffer overflows or denial of service in the native parser.
existingControls: ARCHITECTURE.md: DuckDB for batch only, never for serving
recommendedMitigations: Validate GeoParquet file structure (magic bytes, schema) before DuckDB processing
Run DuckDB processing in resource-limited subprocesses
Set DuckDB memory_limit and threads configuration
Keep DuckDB updated — monitor for security advisories

threats.title: No audit logging — dataset operations are unattributable
threats.description: No audit logging architecture is specified. Dataset uploads, deletions, modifications, and queries cannot be attributed to a specific user. Without audit trails, security incidents cannot be investigated, regulatory compliance (if required) cannot be demonstrated, and malicious actions cannot be traced.
existingControls: CODING-CONVENTIONS.md: 'Structured logging: Use structured log fields (JSON)' — but this covers operational logging, not security audit trails
recommendedMitigations: Implement security audit logging for: authentication events, dataset CRUD operations, spatial query execution, admin actions, and failed authorization attempts
Include in audit records: timestamp, user identity, action, resource, source IP, outcome (success/failure)
Store audit logs in append-only storage separate from application logs
Define audit log retention period

threats.title: No request-level logging with user identity correlation
threats.description: Application logging does not include user identity. Even once authentication exists, if request logs do not correlate each request to the authenticated user, tracing malicious activity to a specific account is impossible.
existingControls: CODING-CONVENTIONS.md mandates structured JSON logging
recommendedMitigations: Include authenticated user ID in all structured log entries
Add request correlation IDs to trace requests across services
Log GraphQL operation names for query identification

threats.title: Celery task execution not logged with initiator identity
threats.description: Background Celery tasks process datasets but the initiating user is not tracked in the task context. If a malicious dataset is processed, identifying who uploaded it requires correlating across multiple systems without a direct link.
recommendedMitigations: Pass user identity as a task argument or header
Log task start, completion, and failure with initiator identity
Include dataset_id and user_id in all task-related log entries

threats.title: GraphQL error messages expose internal details
threats.description: Without explicit error handling configuration, Strawberry/FastAPI may return detailed error messages including Python tracebacks, internal file paths, database schema details, and SQL query fragments. These details aid attackers in mapping the internal architecture.
existingControls: CODING-CONVENTIONS.md: 'Record failures without exposing internal paths or stack traces to users'
CODING-CONVENTIONS.md: Domain-specific exceptions with FastAPI exception handlers
recommendedMitigations: Configure Strawberry to mask error details in production (return generic error messages)
Implement custom GraphQL error formatter that logs full details server-side but returns sanitized messages to clients
Disable debug mode in production FastAPI configuration

threats.title: Database credentials exposed via connection strings in configuration or logs
threats.description: PostgreSQL connection strings containing credentials may appear in: environment variables visible in process listings, Docker Compose files committed to version control, application logs during connection errors, or Celery task metadata.
existingControls: CODING-CONVENTIONS.md: 'No secrets or credentials in code. Use environment variables or a secrets manager.'
CODING-CONVENTIONS.md: 'Safe logging — no internal paths, credentials, or PII in log output.'
recommendedMitigations: Use a secrets manager instead of environment variables for production
Configure SQLAlchemy to redact connection strings in logs
Audit all log configurations to ensure credentials are never logged
Use separate PostgreSQL users per service with minimal grants

threats.title: Object storage URLs or paths may leak raw uploaded files
threats.description: Raw uploaded files are stored in object storage. If the storage URLs are predictable, presigned URLs have long expiration times, or storage bucket permissions are misconfigured, attackers can access raw files directly, bypassing API access controls.
existingControls: INITIAL-PLAN.md: 'Keep raw uploads outside the web root'
recommendedMitigations: Use non-predictable storage paths (include random UUIDs)
Configure object storage with private-only access — no public read
If using presigned URLs, set short expiration times (minutes, not hours)
Proxy file downloads through the API server with authentication checks

threats.title: Martin serves all PostGIS spatial data without access controls
threats.description: Martin reads directly from PostGIS and serves vector tiles for any configured layer. There are no row-level security policies, no layer-level access controls, and no authentication on the tile endpoint. Any user (or CDN cache) can request tiles for any dataset.
recommendedMitigations: Configure Martin to serve only specific tables/layers — not schema-wide
Use a read-only PostgreSQL user for Martin with SELECT on spatial_feature only
Implement PostGIS row-level security if datasets have different access levels
Proxy tile requests through authenticated API or use signed tile URLs
threats.residualRisk: Medium — some spatial data may be intentionally public

threats.title: Feature properties may contain sensitive source data
threats.description: GIS datasets often contain attribute data in feature properties — field owner names, parcel IDs, land use classifications, yield data, etc. These properties are stored as JSON and served via GraphQL and tile attributes without filtering. Sensitive source attributes are exposed to all users.
recommendedMitigations: Allow dataset owners to mark properties as sensitive/private
Filter property fields in API responses based on user authorization
Strip sensitive properties from tile attributes served by Martin
Document which property fields are included in tile attributes

threats.title: DuckDB query errors expose internal file paths and schema
threats.description: DuckDB error messages include file paths, table names, and column details. If these errors propagate to API responses or logs, they reveal internal storage structure.
existingControls: CODING-CONVENTIONS.md: safe logging principles
recommendedMitigations: Catch DuckDB exceptions in worker code and log details server-side only
Return generic processing error messages to users

threats.title: GraphQL query depth and complexity abuse
threats.description: Without enforced depth and complexity limits, an attacker can craft deeply nested GraphQL queries or queries that resolve cartesian products across related entities (e.g., dataset -> features -> dataset -> features). A single malicious query can consume all API server memory and CPU, or generate expensive PostGIS queries.
existingControls: CODING-CONVENTIONS.md mentions GraphQL depth and complexity limits as a convention
recommendedMitigations: Implement Strawberry query depth validation middleware (max depth 10)
Implement cost-based query complexity analysis with configurable limits
Set per-query timeout (e.g., 30 seconds)
Implement query result size limits
Consider persisted queries in production

threats.title: Unlimited file upload size enables resource exhaustion
threats.description: An attacker uploads extremely large files (multi-GB) to exhaust disk space on the API server and object storage, memory during parsing, or processing time in Celery workers. The CODING-CONVENTIONS.md mentions ASGI-layer size limits but no specific limits are defined.
existingControls: CODING-CONVENTIONS.md: 'Enforce size limits at the ASGI layer'
recommendedMitigations: Configure Uvicorn/FastAPI maximum request body size (e.g., 500MB for large GIS files)
Implement streaming upload processing — do not buffer entire files in memory
Set per-user upload quotas
Monitor disk usage and alert on rapid growth

threats.title: Expensive spatial operations on large polygon datasets
threats.description: Spatial operations (ST_Intersection, ST_Union, ST_Buffer) on polygons with 50,000+ vertices are CPU-intensive. A crafted query that triggers intersection of millions of high-vertex polygons could consume all PostGIS CPU and memory for minutes or hours, blocking other queries.
existingControls: ARCHITECTURE.md: Run large polygon ops in Celery workers with timeouts
ARCHITECTURE.md: Pre-simplify where appropriate
recommendedMitigations: Set PostgreSQL statement_timeout for API queries (e.g., 30 seconds)
Route expensive spatial operations to Celery workers with hard time limits
Implement geometry complexity limits — reject or simplify polygons exceeding vertex thresholds for interactive queries
Use PostGIS query cost estimation to reject overly expensive queries
threats.residualRisk: Medium — some legitimate queries on large datasets will be expensive

threats.title: Zip bomb in Shapefile archive exhausts disk and memory
threats.description: A crafted ZIP archive with high compression ratio (zip bomb) could expand from megabytes to gigabytes or terabytes when extracted, filling disk space and potentially crashing the extraction process. Nested ZIP archives amplify this further.
existingControls: INITIAL-PLAN.md: 'Enforce upload size limits'
recommendedMitigations: Check ZIP compression ratio before extraction — reject ratios above threshold (e.g., 100:1)
Set maximum total extraction size limit
Extract in a temporary directory with filesystem quotas
Limit the number of entries in a ZIP archive (Shapefiles typically have 4-7 files)
Do not follow nested ZIP archives

threats.title: Tile request flooding bypasses CDN cache
threats.description: An attacker requests tiles at many unique z/x/y coordinates that are not in the CDN cache. Each cache miss reaches Martin, which queries PostGIS. High-zoom tile requests for sparse data areas generate many PostGIS queries returning empty results, consuming database connections and CPU.
existingControls: CDN caching absorbs repeat requests
recommendedMitigations: Implement rate limiting on tile requests at the CDN or Martin level
Restrict tile requests to valid zoom ranges per layer
Pre-generate tiles for common zoom levels
Configure Martin to limit concurrent PostGIS queries

threats.title: PgBouncer connection pool exhaustion
threats.description: PgBouncer has a finite connection pool. If an attacker holds many long-running queries open simultaneously (via GraphQL queries triggering expensive spatial operations), the pool can be exhausted, denying database access to all legitimate requests.
existingControls: PgBouncer connection pooling limits total connections
recommendedMitigations: Configure PgBouncer server_idle_timeout and query_wait_timeout
Set per-pool limits for different services (API, Martin, Celery)
Implement PostgreSQL statement_timeout to release long-running query connections
Monitor connection pool usage and alert on exhaustion

threats.title: Celery worker starvation from long-running tasks
threats.description: A crafted dataset with millions of high-vertex polygons can cause ingestion tasks to run for hours, occupying all Celery worker slots. Legitimate ingestion tasks queue indefinitely, and the system appears non-responsive.
existingControls: CODING-CONVENTIONS.md: 'Explicit timeout on every task (soft_time_limit, time_limit)'
recommendedMitigations: Configure soft_time_limit and time_limit on every Celery task
Use separate Celery queues for quick tasks vs. long-running processing
Implement task priority so small datasets are not blocked by large ones
Monitor Celery queue depth and worker utilization

threats.title: DuckDB disk space exhaustion during larger-than-memory processing
threats.description: DuckDB's larger-than-memory streaming uses temporary files on disk. Processing a very large GeoParquet file could fill the disk on the Celery worker node, affecting other services sharing the same filesystem.
recommendedMitigations: Configure DuckDB temp_directory to a dedicated partition with quotas
Set DuckDB max_memory to limit spill behavior
Monitor disk usage on worker nodes

threats.title: ReDoS via crafted attribute filter expressions
threats.description: If the API supports user-defined filter expressions on feature attributes (e.g., regex-based text matching), crafted regular expressions can cause catastrophic backtracking, consuming CPU for extended periods.
recommendedMitigations: Do not allow user-supplied regular expressions in attribute filters
If regex is needed, use RE2 or similar linear-time regex engine
Implement query timeout as a safety net
Restrict filter expressions to simple equality, range, and LIKE operators

threats.title: No authorization model — all users have equal access to all data
threats.description: No authorization model exists. Once authentication is implemented, all authenticated users will have identical access — any user can view, modify, and delete any dataset. There is no dataset ownership, no role-based access control, and no admin role separation.
recommendedMitigations: Design and implement an authorization model: at minimum, dataset-level ownership (only owner can update/delete)
Add user_id/owner_id foreign key to the dataset table
Implement role-based access control: at least 'user' and 'admin' roles
Enforce authorization checks in GraphQL resolvers — not just at the route level
Write authorization integration tests for every mutation

threats.title: No admin/user role separation
threats.description: No administrative role or privileged operations are defined. Operations that should be admin-only (user management, system configuration, bulk deletion, viewing all datasets) are not distinguished from regular user operations.
recommendedMitigations: Define admin-only operations and protect them with role checks
Implement role assignment and management
Log all admin actions to the audit trail
Consider separate admin API endpoint or admin GraphQL schema

threats.title: Celery workers run with API-level database privileges
threats.description: Celery workers likely use the same database credentials as the API server, granting full read/write access to all tables. If a worker is compromised (e.g., via crafted file exploiting a native library), the attacker gains full database access.
recommendedMitigations: Create a separate PostgreSQL user for Celery workers with minimal required grants
Workers need: INSERT on spatial_feature, UPDATE on dataset and ingestion_run, SELECT on dataset
Workers should NOT have: DROP, ALTER, DELETE on dataset (unless processing requires it), or access to any future auth tables

threats.title: Compromised Martin instance reads all spatial data
threats.description: Martin has direct PostGIS read access. If Martin is compromised (e.g., via a vulnerability in the Rust binary or misconfiguration), the attacker can read all spatial data in PostGIS — not just tile-relevant data.
recommendedMitigations: Create a read-only PostgreSQL user for Martin with SELECT on spatial data tables only
Do not grant Martin access to metadata tables, ingestion tables, or any future auth tables
Keep Martin updated to latest version
Monitor Martin for unexpected query patterns

threats.title: Native C/C++ library exploitation via crafted GIS input leads to code execution
threats.description: GDAL/OGR (C/C++), GEOS (C++), and PROJ (C) process untrusted GIS data. These libraries have had historical CVEs for buffer overflows, use-after-free, and integer overflows. A crafted input file could achieve remote code execution within the Celery worker process, which has database access and filesystem access.
existingControls: CODING-CONVENTIONS.md: 'Safely parse GIS formats (isolate native tooling in subprocesses)'
recommendedMitigations: Run all GIS parsing in isolated subprocesses with resource limits
Use seccomp/AppArmor profiles to restrict subprocess capabilities
Run GIS processing in dedicated containers with minimal privileges and no network access
Keep GDAL, GEOS, PROJ updated and monitor their CVE feeds
Consider running workers in gVisor or similar sandbox
threats.residualRisk: Medium — native library vulnerabilities are discovered periodically

threats.title: No per-user resource quotas
threats.description: No per-user limits on uploads, storage, processing time, or API calls. A single user (or attacker) can consume all system resources — disk space via uploads, CPU via processing, database via large datasets — preventing other users from using the system.
recommendedMitigations: Implement per-user upload quotas (count and total size)
Implement per-user concurrent processing limits
Implement per-user API rate limits
Monitor resource usage per user and alert on anomalies

threats.title: Celery pickle deserialization enables remote code execution
threats.description: Celery's default serializer is pickle, which deserializes arbitrary Python objects. If an attacker can inject messages into the Redis broker (see T-04), they can craft pickle payloads that execute arbitrary code on Celery workers upon deserialization.
recommendedMitigations: Set CELERY_TASK_SERIALIZER = 'json' and CELERY_ACCEPT_CONTENT = ['json']
Never use pickle serialization
Enable Celery message signing (CELERY_TASK_SERIALIZER_HEADERS)
Secure Redis with AUTH to prevent message injection

coverageGaps.description: No GIS domain expert input on GIS-specific attack vectors (crafted geometries, CRS manipulation, coordinate injection)
coverageGaps.recommendedFollowUp: Consult GIS/geospatial engineer for domain-specific threat assessment

coverageGaps.description: No operations/DevOps perspective on deployment-specific threats, monitoring gaps, or incident response
coverageGaps.recommendedFollowUp: Consult DevOps/SRE for infrastructure and deployment threat assessment

coverageGaps.description: No business stakeholder input on impact calibration — business value of different datasets, regulatory obligations, or acceptable risk levels
coverageGaps.recommendedFollowUp: Conduct business impact assessment with product owner

coverageGaps.description: No developer input on implementation-level concerns — framework-specific vulnerabilities, library defaults, and configuration pitfalls
coverageGaps.recommendedFollowUp: Review with development team during implementation

assumptions.description: Analysis based on architecture documentation only — no implementation code exists to verify actual security posture
Threat severity ratings assume the system will handle both public and private/proprietary GIS data. If only public data, information disclosure severity decreases.
The system is assumed to be internet-facing. If deployed as an internal-only tool, several spoofing and DoS threats decrease in likelihood.
